Define the Teacher, Student, and Notebook and their information flows one by one, separating environmental generation, one-shot storage, replay, and slow cortical learning.
Explain how pattern separation, pattern completion, and Hebbian Student↔Notebook links support rapid encoding and replay from a partial cue.

prerequisiteBridge: Systems consolidation asks how a memory's dependence on brain systems changes over time, not merely whether a synapse strengthens over several hours. Recent episodic recall often depends more strongly on the hippocampus, whereas remote knowledge may receive more support from distributed neocortical connections. Theories disagree, however, about the hippocampal dependence of detailed remote episodic memory. Single-patient cases, lesion extent, and task differences all constrain generalization.

Teacher–Student–Notebook is a formal abstraction. The Teacher is the environmental distribution that generates experiences, not a brain region. The Student is neocortex with a slow learning rule. The Notebook is a hippocampal-system abstraction that stores individual episodes rapidly and supports recall from partial cues. Offline replay presents Notebook samples to the Student again, allowing the slow learner to extract recurring structure from limited experience.

Training error measures reproduction of stored examples, whereas generalization error measures prediction on new experiences. If every observed target contains predictable signal and unpredictable noise, continued training can lower training error yet eventually memorize noise and raise test error. Optimal stopping selects the point of lowest generalization error. Go-CLS transfers according to predictability rather than assuming that every episodic detail is ultimately copied in full to cortex.

modules.title: Recent and remote memory, E.P., and evidence for systems consolidation
paragraphs: The standard systems-consolidation account holds that recent memory initially depends on hippocampal indexing. Through replay and reactivation, neocortical connections gradually become able to support retrieval. Temporally graded amnesia, hippocampal lesions, and remote knowledge provide evidence. This is not the movement of a physical memory file from one place to another; it is a reorganization of network dependence.

Cases such as patient E.P. show that severe medial-temporal damage impairs new episodic learning and has different effects on recent and remote memories. Such cases have great theoretical value but are limited by their single-case nature, lesion spread, test materials, premorbid exposure, and semantic support. One autobiographical score cannot be generalized to every memory type.

The psychological character of memory may also change: rich episodic detail can gradually become semanticized, preserving gist while losing context. Better remote performance may reflect repeated retrieval and schema support rather than complete transfer of the original episode. Accuracy, vividness, spatiotemporal detail, and confidence should be measured separately.

Compressed hippocampal sequences occur during rest and sleep, and cortical patterns can reactivate alongside them, supporting a hypothesis of information exchange. Association does not show that replay is the sole cause of consolidation. Selective sequence disruption followed by remote-memory testing offers stronger causal evidence, provided sleep architecture is controlled.
keyPoints: Systems consolidation reorganizes dependence across systems.
E.P. is important case evidence but cannot be generalized without limit.
Anatomical dependence and memory quality require separate measurement.

derivation.title: Express temporally graded evidence as competing predictions
derivation.setup: Compare simplified predictions from a standard account and an account of permanent hippocampal dependence without presupposing the result.

steps.title: Define a dependence function
steps.explanation: \(H(t)\) is the retrieval deficit caused by hippocampal perturbation for a memory of age t.

steps.title: Standard prediction
steps.explanation: If cortical support strengthens gradually, \(\operatorname{mean} H\) declines with age.

steps.title: Permanent-dependence prediction
steps.explanation: If rich episodic retrieval always requires the hippocampus, detail-specific H can remain greater than zero.

steps.title: Design stratified measurements
steps.explanation: Measure gist and episodic detail separately for the same memory so that an aggregate score does not conceal two trends.

symbolNotes: t is memory age, and H is a causal measure of deficit.
The derivative's sign denotes a theoretical trend and does not specify a particular time constant.
derivation.unitsCheck: If H is a performance difference, it is usually a dimensionless proportion; \(dH/dt\) is change per unit time.
derivation.limitCheck: Near \(t=0\), effects on encoding and retrieval can be confounded, so the design should perturb the system after encoding.

workedExample.title: Decompose a remote-memory score
workedExample.problem: For a patient's remote event, gist accuracy is 90% and episodic-detail accuracy is 30%; control values are 95% and 80%, respectively. Calculate both deficits.
steps: The gist deficit is 95%-90%=5 percentage points.
Reporting only 'remote memory 70%' would conceal the large difference between the two dependencies.
workedExample.result: Gist is nearly preserved while detail is markedly impaired, supporting separate reporting.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Each score is compared with its own control. The 30% and 90% values cannot be compared directly as if their difficulty were identical.

pitfalls: Treating one patient's pattern as a universal law.
Treating a correlation with replay as evidence for the sole causal mechanism.

modules.title: Teacher–Student–Notebook: three roles and the replay channel
paragraphs: The Teacher generates Student activity patterns \(z\sim P(z|\theta _{T})\). In a particular prediction task, input x and output y can be extracted from z, and the Student slowly learns \(\hat{y}=f_{S}(x;\theta _{S})\) using finite-capacity parameters. The Notebook creates a sparse code \(\xi ^{\mu }\) for each \(z^{\mu }\) and rapidly stores the pair \({z^{\mu },\xi ^{\mu }}\). Here z always denotes Student activity and \(\xi\) Notebook activity; the names describe computational roles, not three entities at one anatomical level.

With only a slow Student, a rare experience may disappear before it is learned. With only a fast Notebook, episodes can be recalled accurately, but population regularities are difficult to extract and both capacity and interference remain limiting. Complementary timescales first write online experiences into the Notebook; later, interleaved replay mixes old and new samples for the Student and reduces the overwriting of old structure by new learning.

Replay is a consolidation channel: Notebook pattern completion produces an approximate experience, and the Student updates on the replayed target. If the replay distribution favors salient or recent events, the Student learns a weighted environment rather than the original frequencies. The selection rule therefore affects generalization and bias directly.

The formal model and its empirical mapping must remain separate. The Teacher is not a 'teacher brain region,' the Notebook need not store raw sensory pixels, and the Student is not the entire neocortex. Tests should derive role-specific predictions: rapid hippocampal lesions affect one-shot recall, slow cortical learning affects regularities across episodes, and replay disruption affects later transfer.
keyPoints: The Teacher is the environmental distribution.
The Notebook rapidly stores episodes; the Student slowly learns regularities.
Replay selection determines the Student's effective training distribution.

derivation.title: Information flow in complementary learning
derivation.setup: Represent experience, storage, replay, and Student updating as a four-step formal chain while fixing z=Student activity and ξ=Notebook activity.

steps.title: Environmental sample
steps.explanation: The Teacher generates a complete Student activity pattern z from the generative distribution; x and y can be viewed as the input and output used for learning a particular relation within that pattern.

steps.title: One-shot write
steps.explanation: The Notebook generates and rapidly stores sparse activity code \(\xi \mu\) for Student pattern \(z\mu\).

steps.title: Replay from a partial cue
steps.explanation: A partial cue first completes \(\xi \mu\), after which Notebook→Student links reconstruct Student pattern z tilde.

steps.title: Slow Student update
steps.explanation: Extract x tilde and target y from replayed z tilde, and let the Student reduce prediction error with a small learning rate.

symbolNotes: \(\eta _{S}\) is the slow learning rate, and \(\mu\) indexes episodes.
z is N-dimensional Student activity, \(\xi\) is M-dimensional sparse Notebook activity, and x and y are variables used for a particular Student prediction.
derivation.unitsCheck: The units of the loss and gradient depend on the model definition; \(\eta _{S}\) makes the parameter update have the same units as wS.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(\eta _{S}=0\), there is no cortical transfer. If replay reconstruction is entirely wrong, the Student learns a bias.

workedExample.title: Compare interleaved and blocked replay
workedExample.problem: The Student has learned old pattern A, and new experience B arrives. Each gradient step halves the current target error. If only B is replayed twice, A is not updated; if A and B are replayed once each, which schedule better preserves A?
steps: Two blocked B replays correct only B; A receives no rehearsal against interference through shared weights.
The interleaved schedule includes one A replay, which can pull A's error back after it is perturbed by the B step.
Exact values depend on feature overlap, but rehearsal of old samples mechanistically constrains catastrophic forgetting.
workedExample.result: Interleaving A and B has a better chance of preserving old performance.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If A and B use completely separate weights, the two schedules affect A identically, showing that interference is a prerequisite.

pitfalls: Mistaking the Teacher for a particular brain region.
Ignoring how replay-selection bias changes the Student's objective.

modules.title: The autoassociative Notebook: separation, completion, and bidirectional connections
paragraphs: Pattern separation maps similar Student patterns \(z^{\mu }\) to low-overlap Notebook codes \(\xi ^{\mu }\), reducing the chance that a new episode overwrites an old one. Approximate \(\xi ^{\mu }\) as a sparse random code independent of \(z^{\mu }\); a real system must also retain enough addressability for a partial cue to select the correct code. Structures such as the dentate gyrus are often associated with this function, but the formal model first specifies an input–output transformation.

Pattern completion uses autoassociative weights J within the Notebook to drive a partial or noisy Notebook state toward stored attractor \(\xi ^{\mu }\). The completed \(\xi ^{\mu }\) then reconstructs Student activity z tilde through Notebook→Student weights V. The diagram denotes reverse Student→Notebook seeding by U, but no learning rule for U is specified, so transposing V cannot be treated as the corresponding rule.

Separation and completion operate at different stages: encoding increases distances among episodes, whereas retrieval decreases the distance between a cue and a stored pattern within one basin. Excessive separation can prevent a partial cue from generalizing to the right address; excessive completion can force an ambiguous cue into the wrong episode. The two processes must balance capacity, specificity, and robustness.

The Notebook need not preserve every sensory detail independently forever; it may index distributed cortical components. Lesion predictions depend on the model variant. Disrupting the Notebook should particularly impair recent one-shot memories and unpredictable details, whereas shared structure already learned by the Student should be relatively spared. The term pattern completion alone does not imply a particular clinical temporal gradient.
keyPoints: Separation reduces overlap between episode codes.
Completion recovers a stored code from a partial cue.
J within the Notebook performs pattern completion; V replays \(\xi\) to the Student according to the sparse centered rule. U provides reverse seeding, but its update is not specified.

derivation.title: Reconstruct Student activity with a sparse centered Hebbian rule
derivation.setup: Let \(z_{i\mu }\) be the \(\mu _{\mathrm{th}}\) N-dimensional Student pattern, \(\xi _{j}\mu\) the corresponding M-dimensional sparse Notebook code, and \(P(\xi _{j}\mu =1)=a\). Apply the centered V rule exactly as written below.

steps.title: Write the complete Notebook→Student matrix
steps.explanation: Subtract sparse \(\operatorname{mean} a\) from Notebook activity before multiplying by target Student activity z; M \(a(1-a)\) fixes the field scale.

steps.title: Write the Hebbian increment from one experience
steps.explanation: Each episode contributes one term in the complete sum for V.

steps.title: First complete the pattern within the Notebook
steps.explanation: After U seeds it from a partial cue, autoassociative J dynamics converges to stored \(\xi ^{\mu }\); this precedes cortical replay.

steps.title: Replay the Student pattern through V
steps.explanation: The completed Notebook code passes through V to produce recalled Student activity z tilde, ideally close to the original z.

symbolNotes: V is N×M: rows correspond to Student units i, columns to Notebook units j, and P is the number of stored episodes.
z is Student activity, \(\xi\) is sparse Notebook activity, and a is the mean activity of \(\xi\). This notation must not be mixed with an earlier version that renamed z as the Notebook code.
derivation.unitsCheck: If \(\xi\) is dimensionless, V inherits the activity units of z; (N×M)(M×1) returns N×1 Student activity.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\xi\) codes are independent and sparse, crosstalk is relatively small. If the codes are identical, the Notebook address cannot distinguish the two episodes.

workedExample.title: Compare code overlap
workedExample.problem: Consider three binary sets of active Notebook units: \(\xi _{1}={1,2,3,4}\), \(\xi _{2}={3,4,5,6}\), and, after separation, \(\xi _{2}'={5,6,7,8}\). Count the active units each of the latter two shares with \(\xi _{1}\).
steps: The original \(\xi _{1}\) and \(\xi _{2}\) share \({3,4}\), for a count of 2.
\(\xi _{1}\) and \(\xi _{2}'\) share no unit, for a count of 0.
Separation reduces overlap, but retrieval from a partial cue must still be tested for the correct code.
workedExample.result: The shared count falls from 2 to 0.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Each code still has 4 active units, so the change is not caused by altered sparsity.

pitfalls: Describing separation and completion as opposing operations at the same instant.
Replacing the centered V rule with an uncentered symmetric outer product, or measuring code overlap without testing retrieval from a partial cue.

modules.title: The linear Teacher/Student model: memory error and generalization error
paragraphs: The linear Teacher generates \(y=w_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{T} x+\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\) is episode noise that x cannot predict; the Student predicts a new input with \(\hat{y}=w_{\mathrm{S}}^\mathrm{T} x\). Memory error does not feed a perfect x directly to the Student. Instead, for P stored samples it uses the Notebook-recalled input x tilde: \(e_{m}^{2}=(1/P)\sum _\mu (y_\mu -w_{\mathrm{S}}^\mathrm{T} \widetilde{x}_{\mu })^{2}\), with \(\widetilde{x}_{\mu }\approx x_\mu\) as the limit of ideal recall. Generalization error \(e_{g}^{2}\) is the expectation over entirely new (x,y) pairs from the Teacher distribution.

Early learning moves wS toward wT, reducing signal error, so both training and test errors fall. Continued fitting of \(\epsilon\) in a finite sample can pull wS away from the population-optimal direction; training error continues to fall while test error may rise. This is overfitting. It does not mean that memory itself has deteriorated; reproducing sample details and predicting a new example are conflicting objectives.

The Notebook can retain sample-specific \(\epsilon\) for episodic recall, whereas the Student should primarily learn the stable cross-episode structure wT. If standard CLS replays every noisy target uniformly without limit, a finite Student may eventually encode the noise. Regularization, early stopping, or predictability-weighted replay can protect generalization.

Experiments must assess training memory and generalization on different stimuli. Testing on the same episodes used for training measures only memory error and cannot establish schema learning. P, input dimensionality, noise variance, and learning time should also be reported because they determine when overfitting occurs.
keyPoints: Memory error is evaluated on stored samples using Notebook-recalled inputs x tilde.
Generalization error is evaluated on new Teacher samples.
The Notebook can remember unpredictable \(\epsilon\), but the Student should not treat it as a regularity.

derivation.title: The boundary between memory error and generalization error
derivation.setup: First retain the Notebook-recalled input x tilde. Then assume that fresh x and \(\epsilon\) are independent and \(E[\epsilon ]=0\), and decompose population generalization error.

steps.title: Write the stored-memory error
steps.explanation: For each stored target \(y\mu\), test the Student's prediction from Notebook-recalled input x tilde \(\mu\).

steps.title: Write the prediction difference
steps.explanation: Subtract ŷ from y.
steps.latex: y-\widehat y=(\mathbf w_T-\mathbf w_S)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x+\epsilon

steps.title: Square and take the expectation
steps.explanation: Expanding the square produces signal, cross, and noise terms.

steps.title: Eliminate the cross term
steps.explanation: Independence and zero-mean noise make the cross expectation vanish.

steps.title: Obtain the decomposition
steps.explanation: The remaining terms are weight mismatch and irreducible noise.
steps.latex: e_g^2=\mathbb E[((\mathbf w_T-\mathbf w_S)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x)^2]+\mathbb E[\epsilon^2]

symbolNotes: wT and wS are feature weights; \(\epsilon\) has the same units as y; x tilde denotes the Notebook-recalled input.
Both \(e_{m}^{2}\) and \(e_{g}^{2}\) have squared target units, but the former is evaluated on stored recalls and the latter on fresh Teacher samples.
derivation.unitsCheck: Both terms have units \(y^{2}\). Whether the cross term vanishes depends on independence and zero mean.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=w_{\mathrm{T}}\), generalization error still contains irreducible noise \(E[\epsilon ^{2}]\) and does not fall to zero.

workedExample.title: Calculate the difference between training and test error
workedExample.problem: Consider a one-dimensional Teacher with \(w_{\mathrm{T}}=2\) and a Student with \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=3\). For fresh \(x=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\), find the expected squared generalization error. A stored sample has \(\epsilon =1\) and \(y=3\), and the Notebook recalls x tilde=1 exactly.
steps: The weight mismatch is \(2-3=-1\), whose square at \(x=1\) is 1.
Adding irreducible noise variance 1 gives an expected test error of 2.
For the stored sample, the Student receives x tilde=1, so \(\hat{y}=3\) and \(y=3\), giving memory error 0.
workedExample.result: Memory error can be 0 while expected generalization error is 2.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=2\), expected test error falls to 1, but prediction on this stored sample is 2 and memory error is 1.

pitfalls: Using a fall in training error to claim improved generalization, or omitting recalled x tilde when calculating memory error.
Forgetting the lower bound set by irreducible noise.

modules.title: Go-CLS: predictability, stopping consolidation, and lesion predictions
paragraphs: Go-CLS defines the goal of consolidation as generalization, not complete copying of Notebook contents. Use the signal-to-noise-style quantity \(\lambda =E[(w_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{T} x)^{2}]/E[\epsilon ^{2}]\). It can be simplified to a variance ratio only when predictable signal and noise have both been centered. With high \(\lambda\), cross-episode regularity is strong and the Student benefits from replay for longer. With low \(\lambda\), sample-specific detail dominates, the generalization optimum occurs earlier, and transfer should stop or weaken.

The formal stopping time is \(t*=\operatorname{argmin}_{t} eg^{2}(t)\). A real system does not know population eg, but validation-like signals, uncertainty, replay agreement, or learning-curve curvature can serve as proxies. The model's central claim is that stopping or gating exists, not that the brain must calculate argmin explicitly. Different features can have different predictability, so consolidation may stop separately by component rather than uniformly for an entire episode.

Lesion predictions depend on memory content. High-predictability structure gradually enters the Student, making remote retrieval more resistant to a Notebook lesion. Unpredictable episodic detail remains supported by the Notebook and can be impaired even when remote. Neither component has transferred fully in recent memories, so recent memory is more fragile overall. This yields finer predictions than one age cutoff.

Go-CLS is a formal model and a set of predictions, not a settled empirical conclusion. A test can manipulate training-set regularity and noise, match age and exposure, and then measure how hippocampal disruption affects gist and detail. Comparisons of naturally recent and remote memories alone confound predictability with rehearsal, emotion, and schema differences.
keyPoints: Go-CLS determines the extent of transfer from the minimum of generalization error.
Different components of the same episode can have different dependencies because their predictability differs.
Model-based lesion predictions require tests that manipulate regularity and noise.

derivation.title: The formal chain from SNR to optimal stopping
derivation.setup: Treat the Student's generalization curve over replay time as the objective.

steps.title: Define predictability
steps.explanation: Use the second-moment ratio of the predictable component to noise; if both are zero mean, it equals a variance ratio.

steps.title: Define the learning curve
steps.explanation: \(eg^{2}(t)\) falls during early signal learning and may rise once noise fitting dominates.

steps.title: Choose the stopping point
steps.explanation: Select the replay time at which generalization error reaches its minimum.

steps.title: Form a component-level prediction
steps.explanation: A high-λ component tends to stop later, whereas a low-λ component tends to stop earlier or not transfer.

symbolNotes: \(\lambda\) is dimensionless; t may denote a number of replays or physical time.
\(eg^{2}\) is population or test error, not stored-sample error.
derivation.unitsCheck: The second-moment ratio is dimensionless; argmin returns the same units as t.
derivation.limitCheck: As the noise second moment→0, \(\lambda\) increases and pressure to overfit weakens. As the signal second moment→0, transfer cannot improve prediction on new samples.

workedExample.title: Compare two types of memory component
workedExample.problem: Assume that signal and noise are both zero mean. Component A has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=9\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\); B has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=4\). Calculate \(\lambda\) and predict their relative stopping points.
steps: A is highly predictable and permits longer Student training. B is noise-dominant, so it should stop earlier and retain Notebook dependence.
workedExample.result: \(\lambda _{A}=9\) and \(\lambda _{B}=0.25\), predicting more complete consolidation for A than for B.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A higher ratio means that repeatable structure is stronger relative to noise.

pitfalls: Treating t* as a fixed age threshold without considering predictability.
Treating the Go-CLS lesion curve as an established clinical fact rather than a prediction to be tested.

figures.title: The offline replay channel in Teacher–Student–Notebook
figures.alt: Teacher trains Student online, Student activity is stored together with a sparse Notebook code, and after Notebook completion, V reconstructs the Student pattern for offline replay.
figures.caption: During online learning, Teacher generates training experiences, and each Student pattern \(z^{\mu }\) is stored together with its Notebook code \(\xi ^{\mu }\). During retrieval, the Notebook first completes a partial cue and then uses V to compute \(\widetilde{z}_i=\sum _jV_{ij}\xi _{j}\). The dashed replay path returns the reconstructed activity to Student, allowing Student to continue learning while Teacher is absent.

synthesis: Systems consolidation changes both the anatomical dependence and the psychological character of memory: recent memories tend to be more vivid and episodic, whereas remote memories tend to be more gist-like and semantic. In the Teacher–Student–Notebook framework, the environment or Teacher is a generative source, the neocortical Student slowly learns predictive structure, and the hippocampal Notebook rapidly stores and replays one-shot episodes. Continuous standard transfer can also write unpredictable noise into the Student and thereby impair generalization. Go-CLS instead controls transfer according to signal predictability/SNR and stops at the optimum, so unpredictable episodic detail remains hippocampus-dependent.

glossary.definition: The time-dependent change in a memory's dependence on or representation across brain systems.
Memory for a particular event, including its time, place, and details.
The reactivation of experience-related neural sequences during rest or sleep.
A framework that combines fast hippocampal learning with slow cortical learning.
A set of formal roles comprising a generative source, a slow predictor, and a one-shot associative memory.
A process that maps similar experiences onto more distinct memory codes.
A process that recovers a stored episode from a partial cue.
The reconstruction or prediction error measured on stored examples.
The expected prediction error on new samples.
The fitting of sample-specific noise that worsens performance on new data.
A model that controls consolidation according to generalization and predictability.

commonTraps: A single case such as patient E.P. cannot establish every mechanism of consolidation.
Recent memory is not absolutely equivalent to hippocampal storage, nor is remote memory absolutely equivalent to neocortical storage.
A correlation with replay does not by itself demonstrate causal synaptic transfer.
Teacher, Student, and Notebook are formal roles rather than one-to-one anatomical labels.
Memory error and generalization error are distinct metrics.
Lower training error does not necessarily mean that consolidation is better.
Go-CLS predictions are not established facts.

Empirical observations, standard theory, the Teacher–Student–Notebook formal model, and Go-CLS predictions must be distinguished clearly, and model predictions must not be presented as established facts.

questions.explanation: Facts can be reconstructed from semantic knowledge, rehearsal, or schemas; spatiotemporal and perceptual details must be tested separately. The standard systems-consolidation account holds that recent memory initially depends on hippocampal indexing. Through replay and reactivation, neocortical connections gradually become able to support retrieval. Temporally graded amnesia, hippocampal lesions, and remote knowledge provide evidence. This is not the movement of a physical memory file from one place to another; it is a reorganization of network dependence.

questions.explanation: It can serve as a training sample as long as it reconstructs the task-relevant statistics or targets required for Student learning; the required fidelity is a modeling assumption. With only a slow Student, a rare experience may disappear before it is learned. With only a fast Notebook, episodes can be recalled accurately, but population regularities are difficult to extract and both capacity and interference remain limiting. Complementary timescales first write online experiences into the Notebook; later, interleaved replay mixes old and new samples for the Student and reduces the overwriting of old structure by new learning.

questions.explanation: If similar partial cues are mapped with no continuity, retrieval addresses become fragile; stronger separation also consumes finite code space. Separation and completion operate at different stages: encoding increases distances among episodes, whereas retrieval decreases the distance between a cue and a stored pattern within one basin. Excessive separation can prevent a partial cue from generalizing to the right address; excessive completion can force an ambiguous cue into the wrong episode. The two processes must balance capacity, specificity, and robustness.

questions.explanation: What stops is further Student fitting of that component; the Notebook can still preserve it and support retrieval of episodic detail. Go-CLS defines the goal of consolidation as generalization, not complete copying of Notebook contents. Use the signal-to-noise-style quantity \(\lambda =E[(w_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{T} x)^{2}]/E[\epsilon ^{2}]\). It can be simplified to a variance ratio only when predictable signal and noise have both been centered. With high \(\lambda\), cross-episode regularity is strong and the Student benefits from replay for longer. With low \(\lambda\), sample-specific detail dominates, the generalization optimum occurs earlier, and transfer should stop or weaken.

questions.explanation: During online learning, Teacher generates training experiences, and each Student pattern \(z^{\mu }\) is stored together with its Notebook code \(\xi ^{\mu }\). During retrieval, the Notebook first completes a partial cue and then uses V to compute \(\widetilde{z}_i=\sum _jV_{ij}\xi _{j}\). The dashed replay path returns the reconstructed activity to Student, allowing Student to continue learning while Teacher is absent.
